We additionally calculated the hourly VMT distributions by vocation rather than just source type. For combination-unit short-haul and single-unit short-haul source types, we illustrate them in Figure 60 and Figure 61 as stacked area plots. The background shading color is based on the data density of the source type, as shown in Section 4.1. If an individual vocation did not contain enough data (grayed out in Appendix A), it is not shown for that road and day type category. However, if a vocation is shaded orange in Appendix A for a road-day type, it was still included in these plots, and caution shading colors are not shown on a vocational level. Because the VMT distributions were calculated separately for each vocation and each vocation is given equal weight in these figures (sum of VMT proportion for each vocation in each road and day type chart is one), the contributions from each vocation to the overall VMT distribution for that source type will be different from displayed in the following panel graphs. For example, on urban freeways on weekdays, there is a spike of local delivery trucks’ VMT at hour ID 17 in Figure 60 that does not appear for the same road-day category in the combination-unit short-haul Figure 55 at hour ID 17. By examining the graphs in Appendix A for combination-unit short- haul, we can see that local delivery tracked three vehicles during hour ID 17 out of a total of around 40 vehicles captured driving in that category from all vocations. The local delivery vocation did not contribute much to the overall VMT distribution for that source type, as it might appear from the equally weighted vocation graphs. However, these figures are useful to understand the differences among vocation-specific VMT hourly distributions. Figure 60 shows that transfer trucks begin operations later in the morning than parcel and food delivery and drayage vehicles, which are active as early as midnight. Transfer trucks drive more on freeways earlier in the morning and then peak on other road driving between 9 a.m. and noon. Transfer trucks and parcel and food delivery vehicles all wind down by 4 p.m., with food and parcel delivery still driving a small percent of miles after this time. Beverage and local delivery have some of the most concentrated driving on urban other roads on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., whereas drayage drives most evenly across all hours. Beverage and local delivery trucks start driving on urban freeways around the same time as on other roads but have a morning and evening peak to their distribution on freeways. Aside from food delivery and a small percentage of drayage miles, driving on urban other roads on weekends is more concentrated between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m., with very little driving outside of this time frame. 79 This report is available at no cost
